Newly hatched Gallotia galloti individuals emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a snout-to-vent length of 4.5 centimeters [Lb = 4.5 centimeters], a value that underscores the relatively small size of neonates relative to the ultimate dimensions achieved by adults. Incubation experiments conducted at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] indicate that the total duration of embryonic development, from oviposition to hatching, is approximately 56 days [ab = approximately 56 days], a duration that aligns well with estimates derived from comparative data on the genus Lacerta. The wet weight of freshly laid eggs for the subspecies G. galloti eisentrauti has been recorded at 1.63 grams [Ww0 = 1.63 grams], while hatchlings of the nominal subspecies G. galloti galloti exhibit a substantially lower wet body mass of 1.16 grams [Wwb = 1.16 grams] immediately following eclosion, reflecting the metabolic cost of yolk conversion during incubation. These early-life metrics collectively establish a baseline from which the species' subsequent growth trajectories and life-history scheduling can be assessed.

Sexual maturation in Gallotia galloti is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size threshold rather than to chronological age alone, a pattern common among lacertid lizards. Based on field measurements from the Canary Islands, females reach puberty at a snout-to-vent length of approximately 7.7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7.7 centimeters], whereas males, which typically grow to larger ultimate sizes, achieve reproductive maturity at a notably larger body length of 8.1 centimeters [Lp = 8.1 centimeters]. This divergence in the size at which gonadal activation occurs is consistent with the pronounced sexual size dimorphism observed in the species, a trait that is probably linked to male-male competition for territories and access to gravid females. The timing of this developmental milestone is also influenced by environmental temperature; under laboratory conditions maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at approximately 4 years [tp = approximately 4 years], a relatively protracted juvenile period that underscores the species' slow life-history pace compared to many small-bodied lacertids.

Adult body size in Gallotia galloti exhibits marked sexual dimorphism, with males attaining a substantially greater ultimate snout-to-vent length. The maximum SVL recorded for females is approximately 10.2 centimeters [Li = approximately 10.2 centimeters], whereas males routinely reach ultimate lengths of 12.2 centimeters [Li = 12.2 centimeters], a difference that equates to nearly a 20 percent increase in linear body dimensions. This size advantage is mirrored in the wet body mass of reproductively active adults measured during the peak breeding season in May and June; females at that time have a mean ultimate wet weight of 20.72 grams [Wwi = 20.72 grams], while males, correspondingly, exhibit a substantially higher ultimate wet weight of 34.43 grams [Wwi = 34.43 grams]. The greater mass of males is not solely a function of skeletal elongation but also reflects more robust musculature of the head and jaws, features that are advantageous during intraspecific combats for territory ownership and for access to oviposition sites.

Field and laboratory data jointly indicate that Gallotia galloti follows a slow, K-selected life-history strategy, characterized by low annual reproductive output and relatively high adult survival. Under thermal conditions typical of its montane and submontane habitats on Tenerife and La Palma, where mean activity temperatures hover around 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is constrained to a single clutch per year; females lay one clutch of eggs annually [F_R_i = one clutch of eggs annually], with each clutch containing between 2 and 7 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between 2 and 7 eggs]. This low frequency of reproductive events is consistent with the species' need to allocate considerable somatic resources to growth and maintenance, particularly in a resource-limited insular environment. The extended lifespan of the species further reinforces this pattern; the maximum recorded longevity under natural conditions, again referenced to a thermal regime of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], is estimated at approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], a value that places G. galloti among the longer-lived members of the Lacertidae.

Physiological senescence in Gallotia galloti is not accompanied by a sharp reproductive decline, but field observations suggest that fecundity may drop slightly in the oldest age classes. The species' demography is shaped by the interplay between a modest annual fecundity and a high rate of adult survivorship, a combination that buffers populations against stochastic environmental perturbations common on volcanic islands. Comparative life-history analyses with other Gallotia species, such as the giant G. stehlini from Gran Canaria, indicate that the smaller body size and shorter lifespan of G. galloti are associated with a somewhat earlier onset of breeding. Although the species is strictly oviparous, its reproductive strategy—characterized by a single annual clutch [F_R_i = single annual clutch] of moderately sized eggs—is typical of lacertids adapted to stable, perennial habitats. The egg wet weight of 1.63 grams [Ww0 = 1.63 grams], measured specifically in the subspecies G. galloti eisentrauti, is noteworthy for being relatively large when scaled against female body size, perhaps reflecting selection for larger hatchlings with enhanced locomotor performance and a greater ability to evade predation immediately after nest emergence.
